newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Dole trawl Midwest as Clinton lead grows.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Dole trawl Midwest as Clinton lead grows.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent
President Bill Clinton and Republican Bob Dole trawled the Midwest for votes on Monday as polls showed the president padding his already substantial lead with two weeks of campaigning left.
A confident Clinton did not even mention Dole by name and ignored his attacks on foreign fundraisers collecting money for the Democratic Party from Asian businessmen.
He left the return fire to subordinates like Press Secretary Mike McCurry, who dismissed Dole's campaign finance attacks disdainfully as "a political deathbed conversion."
In a speech in Cleveland, Clinton focused on his efforts to help young people gain access to higher education by making it easier for them to gain student loans.

"Ten million Americans have saved an average of $190 each on their college loans, and even more important, it means you can borrow money for college without worrying how you're going to pay it back," the Democratic president said.

The latest Reuters daily tracking poll gave him a lead of nearly 11 percentage points over Dole at about 47 percent to 36 percent, with about 5 percent for Reform Party candidate Ross Perot and nearly 11 percent undecided.
That meant a drop in the undecided bloc, most of which has been breaking for Clinton. Election Day is November 5.
Dole, striving to reverse these dismal poll numbers without great success, offered what sounded like a wistful analysis of the situation on Monday.
"The election is about two weeks from now and a lot of people haven't focused," he said at a stopover in Detroit for an economic forum with Republican governors.
"Maybe there's not interest in politics. Maybe nobody cares, or they're just getting around to focusing on it."

He was promoting his central campaign promise to cut tax rates by 15 percent, an idea that has yet to catch fire, but the accompanying group of governors served as a reminder that he must now combat rising defeatism in his own ranks.

Wisconsin Republican Gov. Tommy Thompson, once high on the list of Dole's prospective running mates, stated publicly last week that the Dole campaign was one of the most inept he had ever seen. Thompson was notably absent from Monday's meeting.
Many Republicans have reportedly concluded the White House race is lost and are focusing on the fight to hold the party's majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives.

A raft of other poll results showed the depth of Dole's plight. Clinton led by 23 points in a Newsweek survey, 12 points according to ABC, 19 points in a CNN/USA Today poll and 15 in the Hotline daily political newsletter.

U.S. elections are really 51 separate contests in each of the states and the District of Columbia, with the winner in each state gaining delegates to the Electoral College, where a bare majority of 270 votes is needed to be elected.

A 10-point victory for Clinton would translate into an overwhelming margin in the Electoral College. In the 1988 presidential election, Republican George Bush beat Michael Dukakis by eight points and took 426 of 538 electoral votes.

In a speech on Sunday, Dole tried to exploit reports that the Democrats and Clinton have profited from fund-raising by foreign business interests by proposing that only Americans eligible to vote be able to give money to candidates.

His campaign released another statement on Monday alleging that one Democratic fundraiser, John Huang, was conduit for up to $5 million "in questionable and illegal campaign contributions", mostly from Asian companies.
The Democratic Party Friday suspended Huang and has returned some of the money he raised.
But Clinton campaign officials said Dole had opposed campaign finance reform throughout his 35 years in Congress and had himself accepted donations from non-Americans.

"His conversion to the cause of campaign finance reform this late in the game is simply a political deathbed conversion," McCurry told reporters in Parma, Ohio, where Clinton was stumping on Monday. "He is struggling to find any kind of issue, or trying to invent any kind of issue, he can, lacking any serious substantive ideas." McCurry added.
